column2: Mary Ann and Seymour Barab (cellist of the summer trio at BMC, whose basement apartment on West 12th Street is Mary Ann's refuge and the scene of their rekindled romance) introduce Rumaker, without his knowing it, to the twelve-tone composer Ben Weber, a friend of Seymour's since Chicago, recently out of a breakup and unrequitedly in love with Seymour since adolescence. Consequences: A series of visits: tall beers, hidden pornography, erotic stories.
A year earlier, Olson had entrusted Rumaker to Fee so that Fee would wise him up.

In 1953 Greenberg hails Bill's work (exhibition at the Workshop Art Center Gallery) as “the most advanced in our time,” linking it to the Leonardo-Picasso tradition; three years later he compares him to Lucifer, and in the 1960s he regularly attacks him. Formula: “the grand style” and the word “genius” Consequences: A spectacular reversal of critical allegiance

De Kooning joins the prestigious Sidney Janis Gallery, the collectors' mecca on 57th Street, and hangs there the women painted over the previous three years, shaking the art world. A 57th Street gallery; women painted in 1950-1953 Consequences: Success assured, greater independence from the dealer Egan

Bill and the Aicher-Scholls plan the program together; Bill is named director and architect of the new campus on the Kuhberg, overlooking Ulm, the Danube valley, and the foothills of the Alps. When Albers arrived in 1953, work had barely begun.
The Hochschule für Gestaltung opens; Scholl was thirty-three Inge Scholl: 33 years old Consequences: Albers will teach there in 1953-54 and 1955
Four students give Albers handmade Christmas cards, of a uniform size of about 2 3/8 x 3 1/4 inches. Cards in ink on paper, the same small format
Cunningham founds his company during the summer of 1953 at the college. Consequences: He immediately asks Rauschenberg for a set for Minutiae

Murelius comes from San Francisco to teach weaving during the 1953 summer session; Landreau, a former assistant to Dorothy Liebes, is a student that session, stays, and becomes the only weaving instructor from the fall of 1954 to the closing Consequences: Landreau will become an expert in Turkish textiles and director of the Textile Museum in Washington (1971-1974)
The couple leaves the community and opens a photography studio in the neighboring town of Black Mountain.
Appointed music director in 1953; his cosmopolitanism comes from his time in the left-wing avant-gardes of Weimar (the Bauhaus, agitprop theater) and from his experience as a refugee.

Karnes and Weinrib invite Warren MacKenzie, Daniel Rhodes (from Alfred), and Peter Voulkos (from the Archie Bray Foundation, Helena, Montana) for three weeks each at the last of the Summer Institutes. 3 weeks per teacher Consequences: A transformative experience for Rhodes and Voulkos

At Black Mountain, Voulkos immerses himself in the artistic atmosphere and becomes friends with Richards, Cage, Tudor, Wolpe, Vicente, Tworkov, and Cunningham. Richards, a beginning potter, studies with him during the session; then he travels with Richards and Tudor on his first stay in New York, where Richards becomes his guide to the Black Mountain re-created in Lower Manhattan: Cage, Cunningham, and the Abstract Expressionists he admires most, Kline and de Kooning. Consequences: Back in Montana, his decoration breaks free and becomes abstract; a year later he leaves for Los Angeles, with abstraction and experiment fully embraced
After the 1953 Summer Art Institute, Olson is officially named rector, although he had been running the college since 1950.

Fall 1953: the student body drops to fifteen; the dining hall and dormitories close; the students live in the cottages and buy their own food. 15 students; Huss speaks of a “community of subsistence dwellers” Consequences: Transformation into an artists' colony

A fire destroys the great majority of the work Fiore produced at Black Mountain; the survivors include, notably, colorful collages. Colorful collages spared, a bridge between European modernism and Abstract Expressionism. Consequences: Only collages remain, including the work #7-54.

During his longest stay (summer 1953, Summer Institute in the Arts), Cunningham brings seven dancers he had been working with in New York. He completes four new works, Banjo, Dime a Dance, Septet, and Untitled Solo, three of them for a group, and at the end of the summer Merce Cunningham and Company presents its inaugural programs. A stay of about six weeks; seven dancers from New York; four new choreographies. Consequences: The effective formation of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company; Cunningham resolves questions of group choreography.

Cunningham first creates a range of movement possibilities, then uses chance procedures to order them; each dancer has to discover how best to carry out his or her own movements, instead of imitating the choreographer's phrasing. A work reputed to be as hard to dance as to watch. A piece for five dancers; the audience sometimes paid a dime to draw a card deciding one element. Consequences: The introduction of chance processes into dance, a heresy in a modern dance world dominated by the choreographer's personality (Martha Graham).

The college survives thanks to gifts and loans from two former students; Paul Williams is the resident architect. The acrimony and disorganization of the last years erode their loyalty and their investment. Consequences: The couple's gradual disengagement, departure for Stony Point
Lecture “Any Bunch of Notes” presented at the 1953 summer session (transcript preserved).
A music lecture given during the 1953 summer session; transcript preserved.

After settling permanently in Israel, he joins the Technion in Haifa; thesis adviser of Asher Peres. Founding of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, of the Israel Physical Society (president 1955-1957), and of the International Society on General Relativity and Gravitation (president 1974-1977). A Technion lecture series bears his name.

After the Sausalito site closes and reopens on the Embarcadero, the Tin Angel organizes one of its first events: an exhibition of Asawa alongside Jean Varda. Consequences: There Asawa probably meets her patron William Roth, who buys a wire piece at a fund-raiser organized by Tolk-Watkins

An exhibition sponsored by the American Craftsmen's Educational Council; Morley sits on the jury; Asawa and Renk submit objects. Asawa enters a “folding basket” and a “fruit basket” in the category of metal accessories for the home, garden, or liturgy.

Wildenhain approves of the departure from craft exhibitions scattered with mediocre or truly bad objects, suggests featuring Pond Farm (Guermonprez teaches there; “Ida nearly belongs to us too”), and imagines Asawa coming to teach a course there.

A photograph of Asawa's eldest son, still small, crouching and holding what seems to be a globe, in front of a looped-wire sculpture hanging from the branch of a California live oak like a seed about to fall Gelatin silver print, 9 × 9 in.

Asawa's submission is accepted in the first selection; the results are so disappointing that Morley (the director, a supporter of craft) calls a second selection, for which Renk and Asawa do not reapply. List of entries for the first jury, SFMOMA Archives, Box 32, Folder 8

After the 1953 exhibition, when, according to Rauschenberg, their damage no longer allowed them to represent themselves, the White Paintings serve as grounds for other works. White Painting, Seven Panels serves as the support for Trophy I (For Teeny and Marcel Duchamp), 1960-61. Consequences: The destruction or reuse of the White Paintings.
Back in the spring, he sets up a studio and begins the red series.
Designs the costumes for the dance Septet. Consequences: The start of a long collaboration

After an exhibition in Florence where some of his pictures were shown, Rauschenberg follows the advice of a hostile critic and throws the works into the Arno. Exhibited works thrown into the river Consequences: This incident remained the main memory of his 1953 visit to Florence.

In Florence, Rauschenberg sees a painting by Leonardo that marks him lastingly. He would tell André Parinaud in 1961 that it was the shock that made him paint the way he paints today Consequences: According to Alloway, it was more likely the Adoration of the Magi than the Annunciation that Rauschenberg cites.

Rauschenberg asks de Kooning for a drawing, then erases it almost entirely. The result, titled “Erased de Kooning Drawing,” is presented as a drawing by Rauschenberg, with a signature, a date, a mat, and a gilt frame (owned by the artist). In 1976 he explains that he was tempted by the eraser as a drawing tool and by the chance to break away from a model he still admired. A drawing by de Kooning worked in colored pencil and ink; the eraser as instrument; gilt frame Consequences: A gesture of distancing from Abstract Expressionism and from de Kooning, without contesting its aesthetic norm

Interested in the eraser as a drawing tool, Rauschenberg gives up erasing one of his own drawings (it would be going back to nothing) and goes to Willem de Kooning, who agrees with some misgivings: the drawing has to be precious enough that he will miss it, and hard to erase. The drawing chosen is covered with grease crayon, grease pencil, ink, and pencil; after nearly a month of erasing, only faint traces absorbed by the paper remain. Rauschenberg inscribes the title, date, and name on a label and frames the work in a gold-leaf frame bought for it. Length: nearly a month of erasing; drawing media: grease crayon, grease pencil, ink, pencil; gold-leaf frame Consequences: Becomes one of the founding gestures of Neo-Dada; quotation: seeking to free himself from what he had been taught while exploring the imageless monochrome

Two White Paintings are shown there; Cage writes a text for the occasion stating that these works “can be seen in any light and are not destroyed by the action of shadows,” and describes them as “landing strips” for the play of light and shadow. Consequences: The demonstrated influence of the White Paintings on Cage's 4'33".

Boxes of wood or metal (from a Victorian coin purse to Baroque crystal caskets by way of the rubbish heap of any street) containing found objects: pebbles, sticks, earth, prints, string, keys, hair, fragments of mirrors or shells, pieces of wood, photographs; thirty boxes documented on the floor of the pensione in 1953, most of them still extant; looking like reliquaries or ex-votos containing needles, clock parts, skulls, insects, twigs, bones 30 boxes; needles, clock parts, skulls, insects, bones; some materials brought back from North Africa Consequences: They position Rauschenberg as an amateur ethnographer

A collaboration: a tire track. Rauschenberg: Cage did a fine job, but he considers it his print. Cage gently refuses to give up his claim as performer, asking which of the two of them drove the car. A debate over conception versus execution; Cage at the wheel Consequences: An emblem of collaboration and chance

Seen as a provocation or a bad joke by everyone, dealers included. A disgusted critic suggests throwing the boxes into the Arno; when the show closes, Rauschenberg obliges, a deliberate rather than impulsive gesture that implicates the critic in a composite performance piece. Boxes weighted so they would never resurface; the few sold or kept by the dealer will later reappear at substantial prices Consequences: Feeds the legend of the young prodigy

Rauschenberg and Twombly place their works at the Stable Gallery: White and Black Paintings, works of rocks and wood close to European sculpture. A new studio in the spring, with high ceilings, where the Red Paintings begin, the first “combines,” mixing mediums and nonart materials picked up in the street. Fulton Street rent: $10 a month; daily food budget: 15 cents; a bucket in the yard as a sink; quick showers at friends' places Consequences: The birth of the combines

One quiet Sunday morning, with Cage's Model A Ford: Cage drives slowly while Rauschenberg applies black house paint to the rear tire, which rolls over a strip of paper about 22 feet long made of twenty glued sheets. Cage's Model A Ford; 22 feet of paper; 20 glued sheets; black house paint

At this exhibition Rauschenberg sees versions of Duchamp's readymades and six collages by Schwitters; he had also seen the first of the gallery's four Schwitters retrospectives (1952-1962) Six Schwitters collages shown; four Schwitters retrospectives between 1952 and 1962 Consequences: Rauschenberg declares that the exhibition seemed to have been made just for him

Gablik probably meets Johns in 1953, then working at the Marlboro Books bookstore. Marlboro Books, West 57th Street Consequences: For thirty years Johns will remain the person in whose company she was always happiest.
Cage's text '[Robert Rauschenberg]', close to a partial imitation of Breton and Aragon's Dada manifesto, appears in 1953 and is later reprinted in An Anthology (1970)

Rauschenberg trades one of his Black Paintings (1951-1953) with John Cage for a drawing by Matta; he seems to have later used this drawing as the support for a preliminary study for Minutiae (1954). A Black Painting for a drawing by Matta Consequences: The Matta drawing serves as the support for the preparatory study for Minutiae

With very few students enrolled in the fall of 1953, the whole college moves up the hill into the faculty cottages, abandoning the lower campus; the institutes have attracted no full-time students and generated no income. Consequences: An accelerated shrinking.

In “An Open Letter to Bernard Leach,” published in Craft Horizons in May 1953, Wildenhain contests the notion of a taproot: it no longer exists in our time and probably never did; American potters cannot take root by imitating Sung pottery or copying the Japanese rural way of life; the conscious imitation of works foreign to the spirit of their generation would produce only dubious expedients and turn potters into dilettantes or fakes. Craft Horizons, May 1953, pp. 43-44. Consequences: A public riposte to Leach's credo, rooted in Wildenhain's Bauhaus experience.

Carolyn Brown dances eight hours or more a day with Cunningham; the intensity of art, life, and process lived with Merce at Black Mountain redirected her life. Dancing “from morning into the night” seemed “right”; choreographic notes for Untitled Solo taken at the college in 1953

Dawson writes to Franz asking to come during spring vacation and sleep on a cot at the back of his loft; Franz tells him to come; Dawson tells his mother the news; he goes but has to cut the stay short. A cot requested, the back of the loft Consequences: An early return for an interview with a judge in Asheville

When he moves to a new place, his friends gather to paint his apartment; the pictures on the walls are originals given by friends. Original paintings given by friends; the apartment painted by friends

Janis shows the Women canvases; Hess's article in ARTnews, illustrated with Rudy Burckhardt's photographs, appears to coincide with the exhibition. Woman I enters MoMA before the end of the year. Photographs by Burckhardt taken in 1950-1952 documenting six states of Woman I. Consequences: The series and the debate it sets off make de Kooning internationally known within a few years.

The photograph shows Elaine seated in the background and Willem standing in the foreground, self-assured; she poses as an appendage of her husband, as if to attest to his heterosexuality, at a time when the press was accusing contemporary art of homosexuality. Woman I was largely painted in this East Hampton residence. Consequences: Images of this kind shape the couple's public image and contrast with the photographs of Elaine alone in her studio.

The exhibition confirms de Kooning as a renegade in the eyes of the abstract scene; violent reactions from the critics (Crehan, Geist, Fitzsimmons). One painter declares himself unable to paint after seeing the pictures; a dozen others call them deeply disturbing, The Woman a horror and an evil muse Consequences: Woman I bought by the Museum of Modern Art
Ten days after the Janis exhibition closes, de Kooning's first retrospective opens in Boston. Ten days after the Janis show closed

Elaine tells Josef Albers she wants to write about him for Art News in the series “The Artist Paints a Picture” and cover his color theories. Albers replies: “I will make some paintings that express my color philosophy. I will call you when I have some work for you to see.” Two weeks later he invites her to his home: he has no studio and works in his living room, where he has made a great number of small paintings on paper of a square within a square of another color: “I will call this series 'Homage to the Square'”. Rudy Burckhardt, who came with her to take photographs, remembers Albers chasing her around the table to kiss her, to Rudy's great amusement. Small formats on paper, a square within a square of a different color; no studio, working in the living room; a two-week wait; a chase around the table. Consequences: The public birth of the Homage to the Square series and of the article “Albers Paints a Picture” (1950 according to the table of contents, 1953 according to the preface).

MoMA presents “15 Americans,” including Kiesler and Dickinson, two major artists approaching sixty, more or less unknown to the informed art public. Consequences: Kiesler shows his largest Galaxy there, on irregular axes.

Having arrived in America in 1926, Kiesler shows his painting and sculpture for the first time; vaguely known as an architect, mainly for the “Floating City” at the 1925 International Exhibition of Decorative Arts in Paris, he never received a building commission in the United States and rarely exhibited his extraordinary models (Space-House 1933, Endless House 1950).

Kiesler, who arrived in America in 1926 and was never commissioned to build in the United States, shows his painting and sculpture for the first time, including two vast Galaxies. Two monumental Galaxies shown Consequences: The public revelation of works never before seen

Wes Huss casts Rumaker as the Bridegroom in Lorca's Blood Wedding, a long way from his only earlier role, Oogie Pringle in the high school senior play, A Date with Judy, in which he even sang. Consequences: Rumaker feels he is making progress

Dawson meets his most beautiful girl in January; her little knock at his door, a sign of her desire, nearly breaks his heart; nights of love and sleep on his dirty sheets and his little mattress, dizzy with pride, guilt, tenderness, fear, and exhilaration. A little mattress, dirty sheets

For her January 1953 article, Elaine interviews Diller while Rudy Burckhardt takes photographs; they go with him to a charming neighborhood bar where they eat smoked eel and Diller downs one boilermaker after another. At the end, she offers to let him correct the article; he tells her that his dealer Rose Fried warned him: “Watch out for that Elaine de Kooning. She's one smart cookie and she's out to cut your throat”; Elaine laughs, rather flattered to be “one smart cookie.” Diller, much respected by artists for his important post at the WPA, suggests a few small, pertinent corrections, which she incorporates. Their last conversation: he keeps turning his face away to hide his grimaces of abdominal pain; shortly afterward he dies of cirrhosis of the liver. Smoked eel, boilermakers served one after another, a couch full of cigarette burns, the Dillers compared to a Scott Fitzgerald couple, handsome and tall, both drinking excessively but with perfect manners.

Three Chilean architects pose beside Josef Albers, who has come to give his Curso Preliminar at the PUC; the photograph is kept by the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation. Stakes: The meeting between the Bauhaus master and young Chilean modernity.

One day, three details catch Albers's attention: a street sweeper gathering leaves with a long, harmonious palm branch; interlocking metal rings that keep people off the lawn; a mason carefully setting a glass case against a rough stone wall, a contrast that delights him. Words: He exclaims over the richness of the contrast of materials: the fragility and translucency of the glass against the roughness and mass of the stone. Atmosphere: A daily walk between his residence and the university; Albers's curiosity about ordinary design rather than his Bauhaus past. Stakes: Albers's eye turns the street into a lesson in perception.

The meal gong sounds; five minutes later there is nothing left; around the poker tables, they picked the lock of the cold-storage locker to unearth a steak; Olson, 6 feet 7 inches (2.01 m), sometimes joined in, excused by his intense hunger Atmosphere: Cheerful famine and shared delinquency Stakes: The hungry rector's giant body facing the material collapse of the college

The regular pianist, lacking virtuosity, has put the dancers off the piece; Cunningham presses Tudor, busy preparing a Wolpe concert, to come and play “Banjo” once; Tudor obliges and electrifies the room. Words: Cunningham to Tudor: “because they don't know what I'm doing” — “I don't know myself” Atmosphere: Sudden revelation, electricity (something electric, fantastic) Stakes: Converting the company to Cunningham's vision

After days of struggling with Christian Wolff's music, physically and musically impossible, Cunningham drops to the floor as a sign of giving up; Tudor smiles at him kindly and suggests carrying on anyway; they manage it. Words: Tudor: “Well, it's clearly impossible. But we're going right ahead and do it anyway.” Atmosphere: Despair, then serene complicity Stakes: The birth of a work against the impossible

The dance is longer than the score: Tudor plays the piece again from the beginning and has gone only a phrase and a half when the dance ends; he stops dead. Words: Cunningham: “he stopped. That was the end . . . and the result was the result.” Atmosphere: The serenity of accepted chance Stakes: The independence of music and dance

During the big cleanup of the barns, the herd escapes through the fences; Olson and almost the whole community run through the pastures mooing to round it up. Atmosphere: A pastoral farce, at once hideous and hilarious Stakes: The collapse of the college's agricultural dreams

Wolpe, put in touch by Irma Jurist, interviews at the Automat a young man with no experience who has just received his B.A.; they like each other; Schram, who dreamed of seeing Black Mountain, comes down for a two-day visit, discovers Olson's monumental presence and everyone's fervor, but does not follow up. Words: Schram: “I guess they were seizing at straws”; “a company convent” Atmosphere: A New York cafeteria, the clear-eyed despair of a college looking for a savior Stakes: The last search for a miracle-working administrator and its failure

He creates his first dance: standing, and the next instant falling; the rehearsals bruise his hips; he realizes that he is trying to destroy himself and must stop. Words: He remembers having bruised hipbones, and that he was just trying to kill himself. Atmosphere: Physical violence, sudden lucidity Stakes: Art at the body's risk

On a deliciously fragrant evening, Rumaker asks Ellen whether an affair is possible; she answers only that she will be in her room later; when night comes, he knocks at her window, calls softly, and finds the room empty; he feels deceived, his pride wounded, and slowly walks back up the road to his study Words: Ellen, her eyes sliding into a night just as dark: she would be in her room later Atmosphere: A fragrant evening, a black night, Ellen's smile in which anything could be read Stakes: Rumaker's sexual ambiguity, Ellen's protective mischief

Wes reads the whole adaptation of “The Grand Inquisitor” aloud; Duck demolishes it frankly: transcribing is not enough; the drama stays with Dostoevsky; Wes confirms with flat, passive politeness; the rest of the class keeps up a pitying tolerance toward the novice. Words: Duck: no advance, no variation; where are you in all this? Atmosphere: Polite embarrassment, a private burn. Stakes: A first rite of passage: Rumaker's literary vanity pulverized.

Rumaker opens the door to read in the sun and discovers a giant black snake coiled on the railing, in mid-molt, new scales gleaming, dead skin falling to the ground several stories below. Atmosphere: A graceful ritual, spring light, quiet fascination. Stakes: An image of renewal on Olson's return: molting and rebirth.

Olson reads the Pisan Cantos, mocks “the moon is my pinup,” holds up the page with the black ideogram LING, and asks who can read it; Rumaker ventures “harmony,” Olson asks for more, then “Sensibility”: “Bingo!” Words: Olson: “Bingo!”; on Pound: Ez' is playing hip with GI slang, and he doesn't buy it. Atmosphere: A sudden game, the shy one's victory. Stakes: The master's first recognition of Rumaker.

Cutting kudzu and bamboo with bolo knives; during a break, Olson asks what Rumaker is reading; at the answer Carson McCullers, he dismisses her with a “Saturday night” and goes back to the tall weeds; Rumaker blushes and tells himself he agrees, but will go on reading her in secret. Words: Olson: McCullers is “Saturday night”. Atmosphere: Sweat, manual camaraderie, a brief judgment. Stakes: The conflict between the master's law and the student's secret affinities (queerness).

After washing up from lunch, Rumaker sweeps, mops, and sets the tables while playing the classics at full volume; sometimes he drops everything to dance free-form; outside, on the grass in front of the wild roses, Connie and Kate, then Mary Fiore, Bea with David, and Dorothea with her baby listen and chat, as at an informal concert; Connie thanks him several times. Words: Connie warmly thanks him for the music; Olson later mocks the choice of records. Atmosphere: The heat of the kitchen, music spilling over onto the lake and the road, a bright afternoon, a small joy in the routine. Stakes: Simple happiness immediately bitten by Olson's jealousy.

On a pleasant dusk after supper, Rumaker comes down from the Studies Building and hears from afar Olson's laughter carrying over the water; Olson, slumped in a cane chair, legs spread, shouts instructions to Connie, who is clumsily poling the oarless rowboat in which Kate, solemn, watches her mother; Rumaker wants to help, but something stops him; exasperated, her throat reddened, Connie hitches up her skirts and jumps into the muddy water up to her knees to pull the boat through the reeds; Olson keeps laughing and tossing asides to his neighbor behind the rusty screen. Words: Instructions shouted by Olson to Connie (not reported verbatim). Atmosphere: A summer dusk, thunderous laughter, muddy water, thick reeds. Stakes: Charles's mocking domination of Connie, in public, before the eyes of the paralyzed narrator.

Jorge puts on the record brought back from Detroit; Olson, hunched over the phonograph, motionless, his ear pressed close, with the face of a child or of a deaf man discovering recorded music; at the end of the groove he demands the name, then has it played again; then he dances number after number with Arlene Franklin, in a high, supple crouch, small steps near the phonograph. Words: “Who is that? Who is that?” Atmosphere: A giant's stunned wonder; a pinched, brand-new trumpet sound. Stakes: The man of words seized by an unheard-of sound.

Talk about the party; Rumaker lets slip that Charles danced “like a whale”; Olson's hard look pierces him; then a small smile, half amused, half annoyed, a sharp punch to the biceps, “Oh you!”, and Olson heads off to his mailboxes. Words: “Charles, you danced last night like... like a whale!” Atmosphere: Instant panic, then painful relief; a bruised ego hurting more than the arm. Stakes: Care with one's tongue, even in small talk.

A cold, gray afternoon; coffee by the stove; Kline strings together his low-key, wry stories around the metal-topped table; everyone hangs on his words; Guston, a Roman senator, stays in the background. The next day they leave, for good. Atmosphere: The warmth of the stove, the cult of the storyteller, already BMC legend. Stakes: The disappointed hope that Kline would come back to teach.

A rainy afternoon; short of texts, Olson has Rumaker read, and he reads in a timid voice his South Philly story (the innkeeper and the egg yolk); Olson explodes, tears apart the rehash, shouts that he is not his psychologist; Rumaker shrinks, skinless, reading pity and contempt in the others' looks; he thinks of his mother, of the priest, of Madame's “Michel Pange”; Olson concludes coldly. Words: “I'm not here to be a psychologist to you!”; “Quit bein' so much on the side of the angels, Rumaker”; “I can't help you because I don't love you.” Atmosphere: Rain on the windows, pines, the valley in the distance, a tight throat, a feeling of suffocating. Stakes: A writer born through burning; the conflict of the fathers and the queer son.

Olson stops Rumaker on the road and declares that the Bartleby text excites him so much that he wants to go back to Melville; a profusion of ideas: a broadside, a pamphlet, the print shop, contributions; “Mike, you must stop hiding your talents under a bushel basket!”; Rumaker stammers, stunned by so much enthusiasm compared with what the text is worth Words: “Bartleby is Melville!”; “That story is talking about Melville's soul!”; “Mike, you must stop hiding your talents under a bushel basket!” Atmosphere: The magic of recognition; Rumaker walks on air for days Stakes: Rumaker's passage from shadow to light, the beginning of the mentorship

Enthroned on a cane chair in her purple regimentals, she tells of the separate bedrooms (white blanket, black blanket), the children forgotten on the park bench (“Herman! Where are the children?”), and the singsong in front of the painting of the Bay of Naples, cane brandished Words: “See how the little boats swing to and fro, to and fro...”; “Herman! Where are the children?” Atmosphere: Intimate, mischievous; Olson gallant and proud; Rumaker introduced to the visitor, blushing to the roots of his hair when Olson praises his essay Stakes: The great Melville brought to life by his own flesh and blood, before his readers at the college

One summer morning, Rumaker dares go up uninvited to talk about his graduation project; through the screen he sees Olson barely awake, a sheet over his thighs, his hand wandering over his belly and pubic hair; his fists freeze in midair; the memory of his own father naked at dawn in Philadelphia seizes him Atmosphere: The silence of the house, his heart in his throat, embarrassed fascination, the vertigo of intimacy Stakes: The master seen as a father; the forbidden gaze

One winter morning, his father has overslept; repeated honking on the dirt road; his father bursts out in his underwear, leans over his son, who is pulling on his stockings, throws up the cracked window, the icy air on the boy's back, and shouts that he is coming; Joe Harper fires off a shrill gibe from the car; the boy has seen, for the only time, his father's black pubic hair Words: Joe Harper's shrill, mocking gibe Atmosphere: Icy cold, a gray dawn, a hangover, shame and tenderness mixed Stakes: The root of the father figure Rumaker projects onto Olson

After seeing Niagara in Asheville, Olson, more animated than usual, an admiring, lustful gleam in his eyes, talks about Monroe with verve to the boys who have seen the film; later he will comment that she got only has-beens Words: “What did she ever get but has-beens?… Nobody up to her.” Atmosphere: Warm male complicity Stakes: Reveals the ordinary sexism of the progressive genius

Eric drives Rumaker and Merrill from the college to the farm. A radiant Natasha shows them around the house (which looks like a summer cottage); Madame stays in her room, moaning through the thin walls. Natasha announces that it is milking time, sends Eric for the pail in French, walks the guests around the land, points out the reddish brown cow grazing in the thick grass, cries “Rouge-ah!”, rushes across the grass, kneels, and throws her arms around the animal's neck, murmuring endearments in Russian into its twitching ear. Words: “Rouge-ah! Rouge-ah!”; she explains that the cow is young but a good milker, that they have enough milk for themselves, for cheese and cottage cheese, that she will make butter, with whey for the chickens, that they got her at a good price, and tells her darling Rougea how precious she is; she could call her nothing but Rougea, for red. Atmosphere: Thickening dusk, full sun on the western hills, slopes already dark, crisp autumn air; Natasha's voice breaking with emotion, husky, resilient like Simone Signoret's; Natasha as a sturdy peasant figure, unbridled energy; the cow's patient, puzzled gaze. Stakes: Natasha's happiness regained outside Olson's shadow, mixed with sadness: the college misses her energy.

Natasha asks the two students whether they have ever milked; no: at the college, milking was done by machine, with Mantovani on the farm radio. She shows them the motion, in her quick, deft way, and insists that each of them try; Rumaker squats, kneads the silky teats, hears the warm jets hit the pail, feels the cow's velvet against his forehead, the smell of alfalfa and animal warmth in the cold air. Words: First the cow has to be milked; she would show them, and they all had to try in turn. Atmosphere: Cold grass, dusk, the animal's warmth, the novice's sensual pleasure and wonder. Stakes: A sensual rite of initiation, in contrast with the mechanization of the college.

A simple, hearty dinner of Rougea's products; Madame deigns to appear at the table, friendlier toward Rumaker only to extract the latest school gossip; she questions him in Russian-accented French, in a falsely indifferent tone; he answers as best he can in the Russian-accented French he learned from her, the only one who understands it; Natasha, amused, dominates the table with her flood of projects and country lore, as she dominated her evenings at Meadows Inn. Words: Madame questioning him about the doings at the college with an innocent and avid air. Atmosphere: A warm kitchen, Natasha's overflowing gaiety, Madame's hidden melancholy, homesickness for Black Mountain. Stakes: Madame's nostalgia reveals what the college was for those who lived there; the school misses Natasha's energy.

Knocks at the door at dawn; Merrill ignores them; Rumaker says nothing; Jack pushes the door open and finds the two men entwined on the mattress by the stove; he barks the order, insists, stares at the bulge in the quilt, gives Rumaker a sharp look, and walks out, slamming the door; Rumaker gently begs Merrill to get up, in vain; Merrill has gone back to sleep Words: “Gillespie, you know you're on a work crew this morning?” / “You coming?” / “Yeah, yeah, in a few minutes” Atmosphere: Morning cold, fear, tension between gayness and military machismo Stakes: Merrill's imminent expulsion, the fear of exposure

Merrill, a perfectionist, plans for days, shops in Asheville, cooks, sets the table; baby David is in bed; they sit down; Wes comes in without a word, slumps into an armchair, opens a book on Brecht, and reads, legs crossed; small talk about the dishes; Rumaker cannot swallow; no one mentions Wes; they leave without comment; Rumaker imagines what happened after they left Words: Chatter about how good and successful the dishes are; Wes's theatrical silence Atmosphere: A painful social comedy, a mute jellyfish in the armchair Stakes: A lesson in Quaker passive resistance, Wes's silent sorting, Merrill's blindness

After supper, the three of them crammed among the jars and yeast; jar after jar of brew; Bert's knee pressing against Rumaker's; playful caresses begin, Virginia motionless behind her crooked glasses watching them with puzzled amusement; she staggers out; Bert kicks the door shut; they fall on each other. Atmosphere: Heat, rising drunkenness, cramped quarters, an awkward third gaze Stakes: Rumaker's hope of love, soon dashed by Bert's avoidance

The whole class comes to wash the farmhouse windows as thanks for the McCarthy hearings watched at Doyle and Claire's; Rumaker at the top of a swaying ladder, wiping the row of windows, laughing; Olson below, looking up, delighted, smiling. Atmosphere: Lighthearted, companionable, a precarious height Stakes: An ambiguous gesture of gratitude within a hierarchy that looks down on Doyle

After the chicken dinner, the tall, thin dancer in turquoise, facing the audience, performs micro-movements of the hands and feet to a music of sounds; the audience applauds timidly; Olson applauds loudly, red-faced, grinning with pleasure, commenting enthusiastically on the modesty and precision of the gestures. Words: Olson's enthusiastic comments on the sharp, precise smallness of the movements Atmosphere: Concentration, a motionless face to be read every which way, a revelation Stakes: Olson recognizes something of himself in this slender dance

After Pool of Sacrifice staged by Wes, Olson goes up to the cast, playfully slaps Rumaker, and teases him about his priestly role; Rumaker, stung, reflects that he had no other models, Olson included. Words: “And you—you played it like a Catholic priest!” Atmosphere: A public ironic jab, a private wound Stakes: Olson's authority over those he loves; Rumaker's need for his approval

Hour after hour, the dancer in her leotard rubs her back against the pillar like a cat, bending and turning, looking ecstatic, while Rumaker sweeps and pushes the cart around her; sometimes a faint, apologetic smile; Mary Fiore tries to talk to her, but she answers only about dance. Words: Mary speculates sympathetically that there is something else in her: an impossible dream, perhaps the edge of madness Atmosphere: Worried fascination, concentrated solitude Stakes: The price of a vocation without talent

After the surprise party at Streamside, Merce arrives late, gray-faced, with hungover eyes; no breakfast granted by the cook Malrey; a sheepish smile, immediate apologies, and he at once sets the room jumping in exercises; Paul, a little tipsy too, throws himself into it with just as much energy. Atmosphere: The morning after a party, tired good humor Stakes: The great choreographer's professionalism, come what may

After supper and the dishes, everyone comes back in costume; Pat and Michael wait for the dramatic moment to make their entrance; they dance together in a circle, then the men pass Pat from arm to arm to the 78s; Malrey, as a witch, grabs Michael for a foxtrot, her cone nose poking his cheeks, her glasses slipping; Rumaker puts on a toga to pose as Bacchus; Karen Karnes, Amazonian and nude as Ophelia, closes the tableaux on the raft; Wes, stiff and agitated, slips away with Pat through the kitchen door Atmosphere: Candlelit half-darkness, crackling records, sacrilegious excitement and giddiness Stakes: The liberation of ex-Catholics; desire (Pat and Wes, David and Mary Ann); the only Black-white couple in the South

An anxious awakening before dawn, barely any breakfast, coffee and chain-smoked Home Runs; the usual soothing landscape (lake, hills, snowcapped Mount Mitchell) has no effect; Dorothea sits down across from him, reassures him, and brings him back to concrete things: shaving; he goes up to the big bathroom of the South Lodge attic dormitory and takes a long walk in the hills; Mary meets him on the way to lunch and gives him a boost Words: Asked what he has to do now, he says shave, and she tells him to go do it. Atmosphere: Nerves, the loneliness of early morning, self-care regained Stakes: The apprentice sweeper's passage to a writer who shows himself

Fee reads confidently in his strong, slightly stammering voice; Rumaker gets through his part; relief rather than echoes; in a corner, Wolpe is talking with Charles, looks Rumaker straight in the face, and delivers his diagnosis; Charles stares at him with a goggle-eyed grin of delicious perception, then looks at Rumaker Words: “The trouble with Rumaker is he doesn't know how to lie yet” Atmosphere: A corner of the room, a loud voice with a heavy German accent Stakes: The paradoxical key that will free Rumaker into fiction

During the panel, Wolpe mentions his atheism; the woman shrieks her disbelief; Wolpe, bored, his basset-hound face furrowed, cuts her off: “No, of course not!”; amused laughter from the regulars; the woman, mouth agape, turns to her neighbors and keeps a worried frown until the end. Words: “You mine ta' tell me you don't believe in Gawd” / “No, of course not!” Atmosphere: Saturday night, a Bible Belt culture shock against the college's paganism Stakes: A head-on confrontation between European atheism and Southern piety.
